MNI FOREX: USD Softer Following FOMC, EURUSD Edges Away from Key Support:
https://www.mnimarkets/articles/usd-softer-following-fomc-eurusd-edges-away
-from-key-support-1793216481609

* The USD index moved from minor positive territory to modest declines
  following the FOMC on Wednesday, initiated by the FOMC meeting schedule
  changes announced for 2027 and 2028. While Chair Warsh was hawkish on the
  broadening in economic strength, his comments that the overwhelming consensus
  is that the monetary medicine is starting to work some has weighed on the
  greenback overall.
* EURUSD posted an earlier session low of 1.1113, matching its cycle low from
  earlier this month. Given a key Fibonacci level also resides at 1.1111, this
  area will remain a key obstacle for a more protracted move south for the
  pair.
* Antipodean divergence remains the key feature of Wednesday's FX session,
  following firmer-than-expected Q3 CPI in Australia, and a surprise hold from
  the RBNZ. While AUDNZD is comfortably off the earlier 1.2603 highs, the cross
  remains up 1.4% today, with a firm bullish trend reinforced with today's
  price action.
* The UK budget had very little impact on sterling, with GBPUSD largely
  tracking the broader dollar sentiment. EURGBP remains in close proximity to
  recent lows as the cross remains a notable underperformer this month,
  declining around 2%. A fresh cycle low this week at 0.8360 reinforces current
  trend conditions and strengthens the medium-term bearish picture.
* The Bank of Canada hiked rates and communications kept the door open to
  further tightening. USDCAD has declined 0.36% on the session back towards
  1.4000, but remains shy of pullback lows at 1.3969.
* Elsewhere, EURNOK has fallen to a fresh cycle low of 10.3195, down 0.65%
  today. The cross has declined over 5% this month alone on a combination of
  stronger energy prices and turmoil in European (particularly French) bond
  markets. Several support levels have been breached in the process, and the
  14-day RSI is now in heavily oversold territory.
* Highlights on tomorrow's calendar include US PCE & GDP data, as well as the
  October ECB decision.

MNI COMMODITIES: Crude Rallies Further, Gold Edges Lower:
https://www.mnimarkets/articles/crude-rallies-further-gold-edges-lower-1793
213802367

* Crude oil has risen on Wednesday with Middle East geopolitical risk in focus
  after a senior Iranian official pushed back on earlier reports that Qatar
  handed Iran a new peace proposal. Gains extended after an unexpected draw in
  US crude stocks in today's EIA inventory data.
* WTI Dec 26 is up by 2.7% at $102.6/bbl.
* Qatari mediators were reported by Reuters to have presented Iran a new draft
  deal on Sunday to end the war. The draft sets out a seven-day timeline to
  address concerns on both sides, requiring each side to take daily
  confidence-building steps, the official said, adding that the process could
  begin early next week.
* However, an Iranian official said that a new proposal was not presented, but
  that Qatar had put forward ideas that are not acceptable to Iran.
* The trend in WTI futures remains bullish, with sights on $104.40, a Fibonacci
  projection. Clearance of this level would open $106.05, the 2.500 projection
  of the Jul 2 - 23 - Aug 5 price swing.
* Meanwhile, gold rose off session lows in the aftermath of the expected Fed
  rate hold and change in the FOMC meeting schedule, which has prompted some
  broad-based weakening of the US dollar.
* Spot gold is down by 0.5% at $4,039/oz.
* A bear theme in gold remains intact, with scope for a move down towards
  $3,943.3, the Jun 30 low and a key medium-term support. On the upside, key
  resistance to watch is $4,202.8, the 50-day EMA.

more.title: Securing South Africa’s water future requires collective action
more.description: South Africa needs to join forces to navigate the current El Niño crisis and protect one of our most precious resources: water. As the country prepares for a summer season that could bring below-normal rainfall and higher temperatures, the responsibility to secure reliable water supplies cannot rest with Government alone. It requires a concerted effort by municipalities, businesses, the agricultural sector, communities and every water user to manage this scarce resource responsibly. Water is essential to life, food security, economic activity and the delivery of basic services. Yet, as a naturally water-scarce country, South Africa faces the added challenge of managing its limited water resources amid changing weather patterns, climate change and growing demand. The anticipated El Niño conditions serve as a reminder that our ability to withstand periods of drought depends not only on rainfall, but also on how effectively we prepare, manage and conserve the water available to us. South Africa has long been considered one of the 30 driest countries in the world, with average annual rainfall approximately 40 per cent below the global average, making it a naturally water-scarce country. According to forecasts by the South African Weather Service, El Niño is expected to influence weather conditions during the 2026/27 summer season, bringing the risk of higher temperatures and below-normal rainfall. These conditions could place additional pressure on the country’s already stretched water resources, underscoring the urgent need for collective action to conserve water and prepare for potential shortages. It is commendable that Government, through the Department of Water and Sanitation (DWS), is adopting a risk-based approach to identify, assess and manage the potential impact of the anticipated El Niño conditions on water resources and services. Preparations include engagements with key stakeholders such as the agricultural sector, water boards, Catchment Management Agencies and the National Disaster Management Centre. These engagements are aimed at improving coordination, strengthening preparedness and identifying measures to mitigate the potential effects of drought. Alongside preparations for El Niño, Government continues to tackle water challenges affecting communities across the country. The National Water Action Plan provides a framework for improving the reliability of water services through investment in infrastructure, the completion of delayed projects and reforms to address weaknesses in municipal water management. The National Water Access Acceleration Programme is also expanding access to safe drinking water in underserved communities through interventions such as boreholes and the rehabilitation of existing infrastructure. These efforts are essential to improving water security and ensuring that communities are better equipped to withstand periods of drought and water scarcity However, preparedness must extend beyond responding to the immediate risks posed by El Niño. South Africa must also address the challenges of managing existing water resources, reducing avoidable losses, and protecting critical water infrastructure from vandalism and theft. An estimated 37 to 42 per cent of potable water is unaccounted for. Water losses through leaks, wastage and illegal connections place additional pressure on an already scarce resource. Municipalities must prioritise the maintenance and protection of water infrastructure and respond promptly to leaks. Communities must report incidents of vandalism to the police and other relevant authorities. Law enforcement agencies must ensure that those responsible for damaging or stealing essential infrastructure are held accountable. Communities must protect public infrastructure, report suspicious activities and work with municipalities to prevent damage to water systems. Through these collective efforts, South Africa can reduce water losses, safeguard existing supplies and ensure that available resources reach the communities that depend on them. How residents use water matters as well, particularly through outdoor activities such as garden irrigation and swimming pool use. Water users can help reduce this pressure by limiting unnecessary consumption, reusing water where appropriate and adopting water-wise practices in their homes, workplaces and communities. Rainwater harvesting can also supplement water needs for gardening, cleaning and other suitable non-drinking purposes. Water conservation must become a consistent practice rather than a temporary response to drought warnings. Ultimately, securing South Africa’s water future requires all of us. The anticipated El Niño conditions present a challenge, but they also reinforce the importance of treating water security as a national priority throughout the year. Every leak repaired, every unnecessary use avoided and every water-wise practice adopted contributes to protecting this essential resource. By working together to conserve water, manage it more effectively and prepare for future climate risks, South Africans can help safeguard water supplies for current and future generations.
